person.name: Herman_Hollerith
person.summary: Herman Hollerith was a German-American statistician, inventor, and businessman who created electromechanical machines for processing punched cards. His equipment helped tabulate the 1890 United States census and established a system adopted by governments and businesses around the world. He founded the Tabulating Machine Company, which became part of the company later named IBM.

conclusion: Hollerith’s punched-card methods remained central to census work, insurance records, accounting, and other large-scale data operations for decades. Punched cards continued as computer input and output media through much of the twentieth century. The Tabulating Machine Company entered Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company in 1911. The company adopted the name International Business Machines in 1924.

events.title: Born into a Buffalo Immigrant Household
events.description: Herman Hollerith was born in Buffalo, New York, to Georg Hollerith and Franciska Brunn Hollerith, German immigrants. Georg Hollerith worked as a schoolteacher and Lutheran minister.

events.title: Begins Study at City College
events.description: In 1875, Herman Hollerith entered the City College of New York at about age fifteen. He began his higher education in New York City before studying engineering at Columbia.

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, United States

events.title: Earns a Mining Engineering Degree
events.description: In 1879, Herman Hollerith earned an engineering degree in mining from the Columbia School of Mines in New York City. The degree completed his early technical education before his work in statistical machinery.

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, USA

events.title: Teaches Engineering at MIT
events.description: In 1882, Herman Hollerith joined the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Boston, where he taught mechanical engineering. He began experiments with [[punched cards]], paper cards that record information through patterns of holes.

punched cards.explanation: Punched cards became a standard medium for storing machine-readable information before electronic data storage. A machine could read a card’s hole pattern to sort or count records.

events.title: Files Statistics-Compiling Patent Application
events.description: On September 23, 1884, Herman Hollerith filed a patent application titled Art of Compiling Statistics while working for the federal Census Office in Washington, D.C. John Shaw Billings had suggested using electrical connections to operate counters. Hollerith developed that idea into a method for compiling statistical information.

event_class.title: Electric punched-card tabulating system
event_class.description: The system records data as holes in cards and uses electrically controlled counters to tally selected card positions.
event_class.impact: The application began the patent process for the electrical counting method later protected by U.S. Patent 395,782.

events.title: Develops Cards for Census Records
events.description: In 1886, Herman Hollerith developed punched cards to carry separate statistical records for the Census Office in Washington, D.C. A hole in a fixed card position could represent one fact about an individual. The card layout let operators count or sort selected facts.

event_class.title: Hollerith punched card
event_class.description: The card stores coded facts as the presence or absence of holes in fixed positions arranged in rows and columns.
event_class.impact: The card format made it possible to sort and count separate statistical items mechanically.

events.title: Receives Patent for Compiling Statistics
events.description: On January 8, 1889, Herman Hollerith received U.S. Patent 395,782 in Washington, D.C. The patent protected a method for recording separate statistical items as holes in cards and counting them with electrically operated mechanical counters.

images.caption: Replica of early Hollerith tabulator and sorting box
images.creator: Adam Schuster

event_class.title: Method of compiling statistics
event_class.description: Perforated nonconducting cards control electrical circuits that operate mechanical counters for separate or combined statistical items.
event_class.impact: The patent protected the operating method used in Hollerith’s tabulating equipment.

events.title: Publishes Electric Tabulating System Paper
events.description: In April 1889, Herman Hollerith published An Electric Tabulating System in the Columbia University School of Mines quarterly. He submitted the work to Columbia University as his doctoral thesis. The paper described the statistical-compilation system he had developed.

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, United States

event_class.title: An Electric Tabulating System
event_class.publisher: The Quarterly, Columbia University School of Mines
event_class.impact: The published account served as Hollerith’s Columbia doctoral thesis.

events.title: Hollerith Machines Count the Census
events.description: In 1890, the United States Census Office used Herman Hollerith’s machines to compile the national census in Washington, D.C. The census counted 62,979,766 residents. Robert P. Porter served as Superintendent of the Census when the work began.

images.caption: 1890 Census Bureau card puncher
images.creator: Unknown authorUnknown author or not provided

events.background:
The Census Office faced a much larger task than it had in 1880. That earlier census had taken eight years to process. The new census collected more items about each person and required more published reports. The Census Bureau had contracted Hollerith to build the equipment for this work.

Each record was transferred to a punched card. A hole in a specified position recorded a particular item of information. The cards controlled electrical circuits. Those circuits activated electromagnets, which advanced mechanical counters for the selected categories.

A preliminary family count was announced after six weeks. It gave a total of 62,947,714. The count had not used punched cards. Many people doubted the figure because they expected a population of at least 75 million. The complete processing took six years, compared with eight years for the 1880 census.

Most of the original census materials were damaged or destroyed in a 1921 fire at the Commerce Department building. The surviving original population schedules were later destroyed by government order in 1934 or 1935.

events.title: Earns Doctorate at Columbia University
events.description: In 1890, Herman Hollerith earned a Doctor of Philosophy from Columbia University in New York City for his tabulating-system work. His dissertation had appeared as An Electric Tabulating System in 1889.

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, USA

events.title: Founds the Tabulating Machine Company
events.description: In 1896, Herman Hollerith founded the Tabulating Machine Company after operating as the Hollerith Electric Tabulating System. The company leased tabulators and other equipment. It also sold punched cards to census bureaus, insurance companies, and other customers.

events.title: Machines Return for the 1900 Census
events.description: In 1900, the United States Census Office again used Herman Hollerith’s tabulating machines to process the national census. The Tabulating Machine Company also leased equipment to census bureaus and commercial customers in several countries.

events.title: Introduces a Rewirable Tabulating Machine
events.description: In 1906, Herman Hollerith introduced the Type I Tabulator through his Washington, D.C., business. Its control panel let operators rewire the machine for different punched-card jobs without changing the machine itself.

event_class.title: Type I Tabulator control panel
event_class.description: A removable control panel lets operators rewire tabulating functions for different punched-card jobs without altering the machine itself.
event_class.impact: The control panel simplified rewiring when operators changed from one job to another.

events.title: Tabulating Company Enters CTR
events.description: On June 16, 1911, Charles Ranlett Flint merged Herman Hollerith’s Tabulating Machine Company with three other manufacturers in New York State. The new company was named Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company. It was based in Endicott, New York.
events.background:
After completing its work on the 1900 U.S. Census, the Tabulating Machine Company needed revenue in years without a census contract. It pursued private-business applications in the United States and abroad for machines that punched, sorted, and tabulated cards. Flint acquired the business for $2.3 million. The transaction paid Hollerith $1.2 million.

CTR began with 1,300 employees. Its companies made employee time-recording systems, scales, automatic meat slicers, and punched-card equipment. The new holding company carried $6.5 million in bonded debt. Guaranty Trust Company had loaned it $4 million. Flint assigned it a value of $17.5 million. Its tangible assets totaled $1 million. A 1911 stock prospectus listed combined net earnings of $950,000 for the four companies during the preceding year.

Flint described the group as three separate lines of business. He expected any one line to earn interest and sinking-fund payments on the bonds in normal times. He expected the three lines to give the company three opportunities to meet its obligations and pay dividends in abnormal times. The constituent companies retained their established names until their integration in 1933.

events.title: Retires from Company Consulting Work
events.description: In 1921, Herman Hollerith retired from his consulting-engineer role at Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company. He ended his active work with the successor to the Tabulating Machine Company.

events.title: Dies in Washington at Sixty-Nine
events.description: Herman Hollerith was living in Georgetown, Washington, D.C., in his final years. He died in Washington on November 17, 1929, at age sixty-nine after a heart attack.
